title: Slicing and Array Views
goal: Slice arrays with start/stop/step, slice rows and columns, and know when a slice shares memory.

topics.title: Slice with a step
topics.body: A slice is start:stop:step and the stop is excluded; a step of 2 skips every other element, which is the fast way to downsample a series.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(10)
print(a[2:8:2])

topics.title: Slice rows and columns
topics.body: In 2-D the first slice selects rows and the second columns; `1:` keeps every column from index 1 onward.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(9).reshape(3, 3)
print(a[:2, 1:])

topics.title: A slice is a view
topics.body: Basic slicing returns a view, so writing into the slice writes into the original array — the most common source of "my data changed by itself".
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
b = a[1:3]
b[0] = 99
print(a)

debug.title: A slice step of zero
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::0])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(5)
print(a[::1])
debug.error: ValueError: slice step cannot be zero

debug.title: Column index past the last column
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 3])
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a[:, 2])
debug.error: IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 1 with size 3

title: Array Reshaping and Manipulation
goal: Reshape, flatten, transpose, combine and split arrays so data fits the shape an operation needs.

topics.title: reshape
topics.body: reshape changes the shape without changing the data or its order; the element count must stay the same, so 6 values can become (2, 3) but never (4, 2).
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
print(a)

topics.title: ravel and transpose
topics.body: ravel flattens to one dimension (often as a view) and .T swaps rows with columns; together they move a matrix between the two layouts most libraries expect.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.ravel(), a.T)

topics.title: concatenate and stack
topics.body: concatenate joins along an existing axis and stack creates a NEW axis, which is why two length-2 arrays stack into a (2, 2) matrix.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2])
print(np.concatenate([a, a]), np.stack([a, a]).shape)

debug.title: Reshape that keeps the element count wrong
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(4, 2))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6)
print(a.reshape(3, 2))
debug.error: ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 6 into shape (4,2)

debug.title: Stacking arrays of different shapes
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2))
b = np.zeros((2, 3))
print(np.stack([a, b]))
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 2))
b = np.zeros((2, 2))
print(np.stack([a, b]))
debug.error: ValueError: all input arrays must have the same shape

title: Array Operations and Universal Functions
goal: Use arithmetic, math and comparison ufuncs elementwise, and read a ufunc type error correctly.

topics.title: Arithmetic is elementwise
topics.body: Operators on arrays are universal functions applied element by element; `a + 1` adds to every element and `a ** 2` squares each one.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 1, a ** 2)

topics.title: Math ufuncs
topics.body: sqrt, exp and log are the same elementwise functions for arrays and scalars, so one call replaces a comprehension.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
print(np.sqrt(9), np.exp(0), np.log(1))

topics.title: Comparisons produce masks
topics.body: A comparison returns a boolean array of the same shape, and indexing the array with that mask keeps only the True positions.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 5, 3])
print(a > 2, a[a > 2])

title: Broadcasting
goal: Apply the broadcasting rules to scalars, rows and columns, and fix incompatible-shape errors.

topics.title: Scalar broadcasting
topics.body: A scalar is stretched across every element without being copied, which is why `a + 10` is both simple and memory-cheap.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a + 10)

topics.title: Row and column broadcasting
topics.body: Shapes are compared from the right: (2, 3) with (3,) lines up the 3s, so each column is scaled by its own weight.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
w = np.array([10, 20, 30])
print(a * w)

topics.title: Incompatible shapes fail loudly
topics.body: If two sizes disagree and neither is 1, NumPy raises ValueError instead of guessing; that error is the rule working, not a bug.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 3))
b = np.ones((2, 2))
try:
    a + b
except ValueError:
    print('broadcast error')

debug.title: A (2,) vector against (2, 3)
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2,))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.ones((2, 1))
b = np.ones((2, 3))
print(a + b)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,) (2,3)

debug.title: Transposed shape by mistake
debug.broken:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b)
debug.fix:
import numpy as np
a = np.zeros((2, 3))
b = np.zeros((3, 2))
print(a * b.T)
debug.error: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (2,3) (3,2)

title: Aggregation and Statistics
goal: Summarise arrays with sum, mean, std, argmin and cumulative functions along a chosen axis.

topics.title: Mean along an axis
topics.body: Without an axis every element is reduced to one number; with axis=1 each ROW is reduced, so a (2, 2) array gives two means.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
print(a.mean(), a.mean(axis=1))

topics.title: Standard deviation and variance
topics.body: var is the mean squared deviation and std is its square root; both use ddof=0 by default, which is the population form.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(a.std(), a.var())

topics.title: Position and running totals
topics.body: argmin returns WHERE the smallest value is (not the value) and cumsum returns the running total at every position.
topics.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([3, 1, 2])
print(a.argmin(), a.cumsum())
